design_detail: Science report, three printed pages (pp. 912–914) without section headings. Two school-based panels in New York State: (i) a two-phase random sample representative of public secondary school students in 18 schools, surveyed with self-administered classroom questionnaires in fall 1971 (T1) and spring 1972 (T2), 5–6 months apart, 5,468 students linked across the two waves by self-generated identification codes; (ii) senior-class members of the same schools, re-contacted by mail and telephone 5–9 months after graduation (T3, winter 1972–73; n=985). At each wave students reported ever use and past-month use of 14 legal and illegal substances, and at T2 and T3 use during the interval. Lifetime use at the start of an interval placed each student on a seven-step cumulative (Guttman) scale (none; legal drugs only; cannabis; pills; psychedelics; cocaine; heroin), cross-tabulated against the scale step reached by use during the interval (Table 1); students who had used only legal drugs were split by the legal drugs they currently used (Table 2); a four-stage diagram gives transition probabilities (Fig. 1). Results are weighted percentages only: no statistical tests, intervals or adjustment.
can_establish: The order in which New York State public high-school students of 1971–73 took up beer or wine, cigarettes or hard liquor, cannabis and other illicit drugs, and the share at each step who started the next one within 5–9 months, in that place and era.
cannot_establish: That using a drug at one step causes progression to the next (the contrasts are unadjusted percentages that a shared propensity, age, peers or the order in which drugs are offered could produce), or that the same order holds in other places and later cohorts, which the author himself says is probably culturally determined (p. 914).

sample.recruitment: School-based classroom survey: a two-phase random sample representative of public secondary school students in New York State (18 schools); the seniors' panel re-contacted after graduation by mail and telephone (p. 912, running text, 3rd paragraph; References and Notes, note 4, p. 914).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Students in sampled schools and homerooms who returned usable questionnaires (8,206 at T1, 7,250 at T2); the panels are those who could be linked across waves. No other criteria are stated (note 4, p. 914).
sample.demographics: High-school students aged 14 to 18 (Fig. 1 legend, p. 912). The breakdown by sex, grade, race and family education is said to have been analysed but is not reported (p. 914, running text, 10th paragraph).
sample.attrition: Only 66% of fall students could be matched in spring and 60% of spring seniors after graduation; the post-graduation follow-up had a 69% response rate. Unmatched students included a higher proportion of people who used drugs; the T1–T2 panel was weighted only to reproduce T1 marihuana use in the full cross-sectional sample (note 4, p. 914). The column Ns of Table 1 add up to 4,588, not 5,468 (editors' sum; see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Public-school students present in class: pupils absent on the survey days, those who had left school and private-school students are not covered. The anonymous linkage failed for a third of students, disproportionately those using drugs, and the weighting corrects only one marker of this loss. The results describe New York State public schools in 1971–73.

exposure.measurement: Self-administered questionnaire at each wave: ever use and use in the past 30 days of 14 substances, and at T2 and T3 use in the interval since the previous survey (p. 912, running text, 3rd paragraph). The starting position is the step of the cumulative scale reached by lifetime use at the earlier wave.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured beyond ever use, past-month use and use in the interval: no amounts, frequency or routes.
exposure.polysubstance: The scale is itself a cumulative count of drug classes used. 'Pills' combine stimulants, depressants and tranquilizers (p. 912, running text, 4th paragraph); whether medically prescribed use was excluded is not stated.

comparison.controls: Students at lower steps of the scale at the start of the same interval (no drug ever; legal drugs only), and, for the legal drugs, groups defined by which legal drugs they were currently using (Table 2, p. 913).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measures of temperament, conduct problems, school performance, family or peer drug use, or local availability of drugs are reported; the groups compared differ in age and grade as well as in drug history.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: By construction the groups differ in which drugs they had already used; no other drug-use differences are reported.

outcomes.instruments: The highest scale step reached by drug use during the follow-up interval, classified independently of the starting pattern (Table 1, p. 913); use of each drug class during the interval (Table 2, p. 913). Fig. 1 probabilities come from the high-school panel, with students who started several drugs within one interval assigned an order in proportion to students who started only one of them (Fig. 1 legend, p. 912; note 9, p. 914).
outcomes.validity_norms: For the cumulative scale in the earlier cross-sectional survey, reproducibility .98 and scalability .64, above the conventional lower limits of .90 and .60 (p. 912; note 7, p. 914). Self-reports were not validated.
outcomes.operationalization: Progression is a move to a higher step during the interval and regression a move to a lower one; an 'error' is a pattern in which a drug was used without all the drugs ranked below it (Table 1 footnote, p. 913).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests, standard errors or intervals are reported; all results are percentages.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages only (Tables 1–2, Fig. 1). Starting cannabis within 5–6 months: 27% of students who had used beer or wine, cigarettes and hard liquor (N≥342) against 2% of students who had used no drug (N≥467) (Table 2). Moving beyond cannabis: 26% of students whose lifetime use had reached cannabis (N=558) against 4% of students who had used only legal drugs (N=2,911) and 1% of students who had used no drug (N=482) (Table 1; abstract). Editors' calculation, ignoring weighting and clustering, so too narrow: approximate 95% intervals 22–32% for the 27%, 1–3% for the 2% and 22–30% for the 26%; risk ratios about 13.5 (27% against 2%) and 6.5 (26% against 4%).
analysis.covariates: None. The author states that the sequences were similar in both cohorts, in all grades, in both sexes and across family education and race, but these data are not presented (p. 914, running text, 10th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: The seniors' version of Table 1 is not shown apart from a single figure (16% moving beyond cannabis, p. 913); the grade, sex, family-education and race comparisons on which the abstract's consistency claim rests are not presented.
analysis.power: Not reported. Several starting groups are small: the cocaine and heroin columns of Table 1 hold 40 students each, and two seniors' columns of Table 2 hold 8 and 5, so their percentages are imprecise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over 5–6 months, students who had used no drug rarely took up cannabis (1–2%), students who had used beer or wine, cigarettes and hard liquor took it up more often (27%), and about a quarter of students whose use had reached cannabis went on to another illicit drug, mostly pills or psychedelics, against 4% of students who had used only legal drugs. Steps were occasionally skipped: 1% of students who had used no drug used pills without the lower steps, and 2% of legal-drug-only students used pills or psychedelics out of order. These are unadjusted percentages in a panel that lost a third of students, more of them people using drugs.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the legal drugs 'necessary intermediates' between non-use and marihuana and marihuana a 'crucial step' towards other illicit drugs (abstract, p. 912), wording that reads as causal and as without exception. The running text is more cautious: a drug does not invariably lead to the next, many students stop or go back, the number of stages depends on the classification, and the stages are probably culturally determined, which only comparative studies can settle (p. 914, 11th paragraph; note 3). The abstract's statement that the sequence holds in each high-school year rests on data not presented (p. 914, 10th paragraph). The abstract names LSD, amphetamines or heroin as the drugs reached, but of the 26% most moved to pills (12 points) or psychedelics (9 points), and heroin accounted for about 2 points (Table 1, p. 913). The order of first use among students who started two drugs within one interval was not observed (note 9; Fig. 1 legend).

timeline.event: This study: New York State school panels, 1971–73.

Wagner & Anthony, US household surveys 1991–94: earlier alcohol or tobacco use went with an earlier first chance to try marijuana and with starting it once offered; marijuana use with an earlier chance to try cocaine and with starting it (see that card).

Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: in US household surveys 1982–94, 16 per 1,000 young people started a hard drug before marijuana; a model with a shared propensity and no gateway effect reproduced the ordering (see that card).
Lynskey et al., Australian twins born 1964–71: most people who used both cannabis and other illicit drugs reported starting cannabis first; 17 of 622 reported another drug first (see that card).

Degenhardt et al., 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys: the order of first use varied with how common each drug was; other illicit drugs before cannabis were most common where cannabis was rare (as recorded on that card).
Vanyukov et al.: narrative review by proponents of common liability arguing that the stage sequence need not reflect causal steps (see that card).

replication.where_it_stands: The order described here (legal drugs, then cannabis, then other illicit drugs) is reported again in US household surveys and in Australian twins among the papers read for this round (Wagner & Anthony, 2002; Morral et al., 2002; Lynskey et al., 2003), while cross-national surveys show that the order depends on how common each drug is (Degenhardt et al., 2010, as recorded on its card). The descriptive sequence is replicated in settings like this one; whether it reflects a causal step, a shared propensity or the order in which drugs are offered remains open, and the reading list notes that no single design separates the three explanations.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse research grant DA-00064 (References and Notes, note 12, p. 914).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author: Biometrics Research, New York State Psychiatric Institute, and School of Public Health and Department of Psychiatry, Columbia University (p. 914).

what_would_settle_it: A cohort followed from before any drug use, recording first offers and first use of each drug as they happen (in months, not recalled intervals), with propensity measured at baseline (conduct problems, family and peer use), analysed so that the order of opportunities and a shared liability are separated from any effect of the earlier drug, and repeated in places where cannabis is not the most available illicit drug.

domains.note: No adjustment of any kind. Students at different steps differ in age, grade, peers, family background and propensity to use drugs, none of which enters the comparisons; a shared liability or the order in which drugs are offered would produce the same pattern.
Self-reported ever use in a classroom questionnaire with broad classes ('legal drugs', 'pills'); the cumulative scale fits well, but individual reports were not checked.
Only 66% of students were linked across waves (60% of seniors), unmatched students used drugs more, and the weighting corrects only T1 marihuana prevalence (note 4, p. 914).
Table 1 accounts for 4,588 of the 5,468 panel students (editors' sum); how the remainder (non-cumulative starting patterns, missing answers or weighting) was handled is not described.

Use during the interval is self-reported; for students who started several drugs within one 5–6-month interval the order was not observed, and for legal drugs it was assigned by assumption (note 9; Fig. 1 legend).
The seniors' table and the grade, sex, family-education and race analyses are not shown; Fig. 1 and Table 2 disagree on two values (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Judged as evidence that using one drug leads to the next (the gateway question), the study has no control for confounding at all, and a third of the panel was lost selectively. As a description, it is a well-sampled two-wave panel showing the order of first use and short-term transition rates in New York State public schools in 1971–73. Citable for that order, for the transition percentages with their denominators, and for the author's own caveat that the stages are probably culturally determined; not citable as evidence that legal drugs or cannabis cause later drug use, nor for the size of any such effect.

key_findings.finding: Two New York State school panels: 5,468 students linked between fall 1971 and spring 1972 (5–6 months) and 985 graduated seniors re-contacted 5–9 months after graduation; usable questionnaires were obtained from 8,206 students at T1 and 7,250 at T2.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 3rd paragraph (p. 912, middle column); References and Notes, note 4 (p. 914)

key_findings.finding: Linkage by self-generated codes matched 66% of fall students in the spring and 60% of spring seniors after graduation (post-graduation response rate 69%); unmatched students included more people who used drugs, and the T1–T2 panel was weighted to reproduce T1 marihuana use in the full cross-sectional sample.

In the earlier cross-sectional survey, lifetime use fitted a seven-step cumulative scale (none; legal drugs; cannabis; pills; psychedelics; cocaine; heroin) with reproducibility .98 and scalability .64, against conventional minima of .90 and .60.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 4th paragraph (p. 912, right column); References and Notes, note 7 (p. 914)

key_findings.finding: Of 482 students who had used no drug by fall 1971, 62% used none in the next 5–6 months, 36% used legal drugs only, 1% used legal drugs and cannabis, and 1% used pills without the lower steps (out of order); none used cannabis without legal drugs.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column (i); running text, 7th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Of 2,911 students who had used only legal drugs, 79% stayed at legal drugs, 10% used no drug in the interval, 7% added cannabis, 2% reached pills with a complete cumulative pattern including cannabis, and 2% reached pills (1%) or psychedelics (1%) out of order, which the author reads as going to other illicit drugs without cannabis (2–3% in each cohort).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column (ii); running text, 8th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Of 558 students whose lifetime use had reached cannabis but no further, 26% moved beyond cannabis within 5–6 months (16% among graduated seniors, not tabulated). Highest step reached in Table 1: pills 12% (9% in cumulative order plus 3% out of order), psychedelics 9% (5% plus 4%), cocaine 2% (out of order), heroin 2% (1% plus 1%); 19% used only legal drugs in the interval and 56% stayed at cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column (iii) and footnote; running text, 8th paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: The printed cells beyond cannabis sum to 25% (editors' sum), within rounding of the stated 26%. Approximate 95% interval for 26% of 558: 22–30% (editors' calculation, ignoring weighting and clustering).

key_findings.finding: No student who had used an illicit drug by T1 used no drug at all in the interval; regression went to lower illicit steps or to legal drugs. Out-of-order patterns rose with the starting step: 1% (none), 2% (legal), 11% (cannabis), 12% (pills), 18% (psychedelics), 28% (cocaine) and 34% (heroin). Of the 40 students at the heroin step, 42% used heroin in the interval, 23 of those percentage points without some lower-step drugs.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 6th paragraph (begins p. 912, right column; continues p. 913, left column); Table 1

key_findings.finding: Starting cannabis between fall 1971 and spring 1972, by legal-drug pattern at T1: never used any drug 2% (N≥467); used legal drugs but not currently 5% (N≥694); beer or wine only 4% (N≥731); cigarettes only 16% (N≥70); cigarettes plus beer or wine 16% (N≥356); hard liquor plus beer or wine 11% (N≥429); all three 27% (N≥342). Starting other illicit drugs in the same groups: 1%, 2%, 2%, 7%, 6%, 4% and 11%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, New York State total high school panel sample (T1 to T2)
key_findings.note: Approximate 95% intervals 22–32% for the 27% and 1–3% for the 2% (editors' calculation, ignoring weighting); risk ratio about 13.5 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Graduated seniors, spring 1972 to winter 1972–73: starting cannabis 6% of those who had used no drug (N≥62), 11% after beer or wine only (N≥103), 18% after cigarettes plus beer or wine (N≥16), 18% after hard liquor plus beer or wine (N≥206) and 29% after all three (N≥91); other illicit drugs 2%, 2%, 6%, 2% and 4%. The columns with N≥8 and N≥5 are largely or wholly empty.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, graduated seniors panel sample (T2 to T3)

key_findings.finding: Among the legal drugs, most students who started one began with beer or wine; exclusive starts with cigarettes or hard liquor were rare (5% and 2% in the high-school cohort, base not stated). Students using beer or wine took up hard liquor two to three times as often as cigarettes (33% against 14%; seniors 41% against 14%); 68% of students using cigarettes and beer or wine took up hard liquor, against 21% of students using hard liquor and beer or wine taking up cigarettes. The author states that no student in either cohort went from beer or wine to illicit drugs without hard liquor or cigarettes, and describes the associations of tobacco and hard liquor with starting marihuana as independent and additive (no test shown).
key_findings.locator: Running text, 9th paragraph (begins p. 913, left column; ends p. 914, left column); Table 2; References and Notes, note 8 (p. 914)

key_findings.finding: Fig. 1 (high-school panel, ages 14 to 18) gives stage probabilities: no use to beer or wine .28; beer or wine to hard liquor .32 and to cigarettes .08; hard liquor to cigarettes .21; cigarettes to hard liquor .68; marihuana .16 from the hard-liquor path, .27 after both and .11 from the cigarettes path; marihuana to other illicit drugs .26. Students who started more than one drug within the interval were placed in order by assumption.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1 and legend (p. 912); References and Notes, note 9 (p. 914)
key_findings.note: Values read from a 300-dpi crop of the rendered figure. The two marihuana values for the single-legal-drug paths appear transposed relative to Table 2 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The author states that the patterns were strikingly similar in both cohorts, in all grades, in both sexes and independent of family educational background and race, but the data are not presented.

The author's caveats: a drug does not invariably lead to those higher in the sequence, many students stop at a stage and many regress, the number of stages depends on how drug behaviours are classified, and the stages are probably culturally determined, a question only comparative and cross-cultural studies can answer.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 11th paragraph (left column); References and Notes, note 3

key_findings.finding: Methodological point made by the author: since each stage is a cumulative pattern, people at a stage should be compared with those who reached the preceding stage, not with the whole population, or characteristics of the earlier stage will be misattributed to the later drug.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1 places .16 on the marihuana path after hard liquor and .11 on the path after cigarettes, whereas Table 2 (T1 to T2) gives 11% starting cannabis after hard liquor plus beer or wine and 16% after cigarettes plus beer or wine. The figure's .21 and .68 match those same two Table 2 columns, so the two marihuana values appear transposed in the figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which legal drug went with more cannabis initiation should be taken from Table 2 (cigarettes); Fig. 1 should not be cited for that comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The column Ns of Table 1 sum to 4,588 against a stated panel of 5,468 (editors' sum), with no explanation (non-cumulative starting patterns, missing answers or weighted Ns could account for it). The text's figure of 82% of students who had used legal drugs cannot be derived from Table 1, where 4,106 of 4,588 (89.5%, editors' calculation) had at least used legal drugs by T1; its base is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators behind the percentages are uncertain, and up to 16% of the panel is unaccounted for in the main table.

reporting_issues.issue: In the abstract, the group in which 1% moved to other illicit drugs is printed with a garbled label (a 'nondrug' group qualified by marihuana); Table 1 shows the 1% refers to students who had used no drug at T1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the figure should be attributed to students who had used no drug, from Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Students who took up cannabis and another illicit drug within the same 5–6-month interval appear in Table 1 as following the cumulative order, although the order in which they started the two drugs was not observed; the paper describes an ordering assumption only for legal drugs (note 9) and for Fig. 1 (legend).
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the evidence that cannabis precedes other illicit drugs is assumed rather than observed; how large that part is cannot be told from the paper.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, scan of Science 190, 28 November 1975), pp. 912–914 (all three pages of the report; poor text layer, so the rendered pages were the source; Tables 1–2, Fig. 1, the abstract and the notes checked on pages rendered at 150 and 300 dpi; parts of adjacent articles on pp. 912 and 914 not read; no supplement)
